Sensory Glove-Based Surgical Robot User.narr: A surgeon's hands have tremor and natural coarseness. A sensory glove maps gross finger motions to scaled-down instrument displacements, filtering out involuntary oscillation while preserving intent. Haptic feedback closes the loop, letting the surgeon feel tissue resistance through the console.
Sensory Glove-Based Surgical Robot User.how: The glove's flex sensors capture finger joint angles at ~100 Hz. A scaling layer reduces hand displacement by a fixed factor (typically 3:1 to 10:1), so a 20 mm hand motion becomes 2–6 mm at the instrument tip. A bandpass filter removes frequencies >6 Hz (tremor) before sending the signal to the actuators. Haptic motors at the console reproduce scaled forces: 0.1 N at the tip becomes 0.5–1 N felt at the glove, creating the illusion of direct contact. The kinematic chain (glove → scaler → tremor filter → actuator → instrument) must complete within 5 ms or the surgeon perceives lag.

AR-Based Endoscope Control for Laparosco.narr: Steering an endoscope by hand is unintuitive when you cannot see what you are steering toward. Augmented-reality overlays project a target region onto the live endoscopic image, and the surgeon navigates the scope toward that target while watching the overlay move with the instrument. Visual guidance replaces mental geometry.
AR-Based Endoscope Control for Laparosco.how: A preoperative 3D model or intraoperative segmentation defines a target anatomy (e.g., the gallbladder in a cholecystectomy). The system tracks endoscope pose using SLAM or electromagnetic tracking, then projects the target region onto the live video stream as a transparent overlay or reticle. As the surgeon moves the scope, the overlay updates in real time, showing whether the tip is pointing toward or away from the target. A distance metric (e.g., 3D point-to-plane error from tip to target surface) provides numeric feedback. The surgeon steers iteratively, using the visual guide to reduce error faster than freehand navigation would allow.

MEDiC: Autonomous Exposure for Robotic D.narr: Tissue must be positioned correctly for the next cut—not too deep, not pulling away—and doing this manually wastes time. A learned policy observes the surgical field and autonomously repositions tissue for the optimal cutting angle and depth, treating positioning as a subtask the robot can own.
MEDiC: Autonomous Exposure for Robotic D.how: The system is trained end-to-end on video of dissection tasks, learning to associate the current tissue configuration (imaged) with the command that best repositions the tissue for the next step. Inputs are the endoscopic video and the current phase of the procedure. The learned policy outputs a motion command: direction, speed, and hold duration. Before executing, a safety layer checks that the motion stays within a segmented safe zone (away from critical structures). The robot applies the motion, watches the result, and confirms via segmentation that the tissue is now in the desired position. Error signals (position not where expected, or motion into a forbidden zone) trigger backoff and re-planning.

DRL Semi-Autonomous Magnetic Micro-Robot.narr: A magnetic micro-robot moves through blood vessels under external magnetic field control, but the surgeon's manual input is slow and error-prone. Deep reinforcement learning shares steering: the learned policy handles routine course corrections, while the surgeon retains high-level waypoint commands. The surgeon sets a target; the RL agent does the fine-grained steering.
DRL Semi-Autonomous Magnetic Micro-Robot.how: The micro-robot is a ferromagnetic capsule steered by an external coil array generating a rotating magnetic field. The surgeon provides high-level commands (target vessel segment, go left/right at the next bifurcation) via a console interface. A trained RL agent observes the robot's position (tracked by fluoroscopy or ultrasound) and the vessel geometry ahead, and issues continuous low-level steering actions (coil currents) to follow the intended path. The RL policy is trained in simulation on thousands of procedurally generated vessel trees, learning to balance responsiveness with stability. Sim-to-real transfer uses domain randomization (vessel diameter ±20%, friction ±30%). The surgeon can override at any time by issuing a new high-level command; the policy adapts immediately.

Advancing Dense Endoscopic Reconstructio.narr: Endoscopes see a narrow, deforming, specular-filled view of the lumen. Extracting a stable 3D reconstruction is SLAM on hard mode: 2D Gaussians splat onto a deformable surface, tracking features through wet, moving walls. The result is a usable map of the surgical cavity that guides planning and tracking.
Advancing Dense Endoscopic Reconstructio.how: The algorithm processes the monocular endoscope video frame-by-frame. High-intensity pixels (specular reflections, brightness > 240/255) are masked before feature extraction. SIFT or ORB keypoints are tracked across 5-frame windows using Lucas-Kanade, building a sparse point cloud. Depth is recovered by exploiting the known instrument diameter (an 8 mm trocar shaft in the view) as a photometric scale anchor. As new frames arrive, the system maintains 2D Gaussian splats anchored to the sparse points; each splat covers a local surface region. An as-rigid-as-possible deformation prior (λ ≈ 0.8) regularizes the surface to stay locally rigid across frames, fighting breathing and peristalsis. On modern hardware (RTX 3090), per-frame refit takes ~12 ms. The output is a continuously updated 3D mesh of the lumen, stable enough for surgical planning.

Bilateral Structural Intensity-Depth Reg.narr: An endoscope that flexes distorts both the RGB image and any depth estimate. Joint registration of intensity and depth channels compensates for flex, using spatial coupling to keep the two modalities aligned. The result is a coherent perception of space despite the instrument bending.
Bilateral Structural Intensity-Depth Reg.how: The system processes synchronized RGB and depth frames from the endoscope. Flex (or hysteresis) in the insertion tube causes a time-varying misalignment between the RGB optical center and the depth sensor optical center. An iterative registration algorithm solves for a per-frame transformation that aligns edges in the intensity image with edges in the depth image. The key constraint is bilateral consistency: intensity features must be explained by depth discontinuities, and depth discontinuities must be consistent with intensity gradients. Optimization alternates between estimating the flex transformation and updating a spatial deformation model of the lumen. This coupled approach outperforms registering RGB and depth independently, because the flex is systematic but time-varying—enforcing bilateral agreement makes the estimate more stable against noise.

Remote: Real-Time Endoscope Ego-Motion E.narr: Knowing where the endoscope is and where it is moving is essential for surgical navigation and tool tracking. Fast monocular ego-motion estimation computes camera motion in real-time from the endoscope video alone, without relying on external tracking, giving the surgeon a live picture of the instrument's position inside the lumen.
Remote: Real-Time Endoscope Ego-Motion E.how: The system uses optical flow and keypoint tracking on the monocular endoscope video. Consecutive frames are aligned via a two-point RANSAC algorithm that estimates the camera rotation and translation. Specular highlights are masked beforehand to avoid spurious matches. The method exploits temporal coherence: in a smooth endoscope insertion, the motion between frames is small (less than 5 mm translocation, less than 5 degrees rotation). A Kalman filter fuses frame-to-frame estimates, predicting the next ego-motion and correcting for tracking outliers. The entire pipeline (optical flow, RANSAC, Kalman update) runs in less than 1 ms per frame on CPU, allowing real-time streaming at 30 fps. Output is a smooth 6-DOF pose (x,y,z, roll,pitch,yaw) of the endoscope in the lumen, which downstream modules use for tool-in-lumen localization and augmented-reality overlay positioning.

SLAM Assisted 3D Tracking for Laparoscop.narr: Surgical instruments deform and drift in the laparoscopic view. SLAM builds a map of the surgical cavity once, then uses that fixed map to stabilize and predict instrument positions, fighting the visual drift that plagues frame-to-frame tracking alone.
SLAM Assisted 3D Tracking for Laparoscop.how: The system runs two parallel threads. The first is a real-time SLAM backend: sparse keypoint features are matched across the video stream, and a bundle-adjustment step maintains a metrically accurate 3D map of the tissue. Because the tissue itself deforms, the SLAM map is treated as semi-static: it gets a local update every 10–20 frames but is not globally optimized every frame (to avoid over-correcting for deformation). The second thread is instrument tracking. The instrument (e.g., a grasper or dissector) is tracked frame-to-frame via template matching or Hough circles (for the instrument shaft). Without map context, this accumulates drift. The innovation is to project the instrument's 3D position into the SLAM map: if the instrument's tracked position projects to an invalid region (inside tissue or far from any keypoint), the track is corrected to the nearest valid position in the SLAM map. This map-informed correction reduces tracking drift by ~70% compared to frame-to-frame tracking alone.

Steerable Tape-Spring Needle for Autonom.narr: Bevel-tip needles bend as they advance, but the radius of curvature is limited by tissue stiffness. A tape-spring mechanism pre-bends the needle, enabling tighter-radius turns that can thread around obstacles bevel-only designs cannot reach.
Steerable Tape-Spring Needle for Autonom.how: A tape-spring is a thin, curved metal ribbon that naturally wants to curl. Wrapped helically around a flexible tube (the needle shaft), it stores elastic energy and tries to coil the shaft into a tight helix. As the needle advances, friction from the tissue releases this stored energy, and the needle tip follows a curved path. Unlike a passive bevel tip (which generates curvature only from tissue stiffness), the tape-spring actively bends the needle. By tuning the initial curvature and spring stiffness, the designer can achieve a needle curvature radius of 30–50 mm, vs. 80–150 mm for bevel-only designs. The control law is spinning duty-cycle: spin the needle to go straight (friction prevents the spring from coiling), stop spinning to allow the spring to curve. Closed-loop steering via ultrasound feedback confirms that turns meet the planned angle. This trades mechanical complexity for access to targets (e.g., lung nodules) that require sharper bends than classical needle steering offers.

Resolution-Optimal Motion Planning for N.narr: Steering a needle through lung to a biopsy target requires a path that is accurate (tip lands near the target) with the fewest control steps (minimize insertions and spin-stop cycles). Resolution-optimal planning solves for the path that meets accuracy needs with minimum control effort. Fewer steps mean less tissue trauma.
Resolution-Optimal Motion Planning for N.how: The system takes as input a 3D ultrasound map of the lung, the needle's kinematics (curvature radius as a function of spin/stop commands, tissue stiffness estimates), and a target position within ±2 mm. A motion-planning algorithm searches over sequences of control steps (spin-N-steps, stop-M-steps, repeat). Each sequence is simulated forward using the needle kinematics model: given tissue stiffness, the curvature is deterministic; the cumulative trajectory is computed via numerical integration of the Cosserat rod model. Simulated trajectories are scored on (1) distance of final tip position to the target (must be < 2 mm) and (2) number of control steps (minimized). A* or RRT* finds the Pareto-optimal plan: the one with fewest steps that still hits the accuracy requirement. The planner runs offline before insertion; during insertion, an MPC layer updates the model using real deflection feedback and re-plans if drift exceeds a threshold.

Model Predictive Control for 3D Steerabl.narr: A needle path plan must adapt as the needle advances through heterogeneous tissue with varying stiffness. MPC tracks the planned path by predicting the next few steps ahead and correcting the control input when actual deflection differs from the model. Real-time replanning keeps accuracy under 2 mm.
Model Predictive Control for 3D Steerabl.how: MPC maintains an internal model of needle kinematics: curvature as a function of tissue stiffness k, bevel angle, and spindle speed. At each control cycle (every 1 mm of insertion), the controller observes the actual needle position (via ultrasound or fluoroscopy). If position deviates from the planned path by more than ±0.5 mm, the controller solves a finite-horizon optimization problem: what sequence of spin/stop commands over the next 10 steps (10 mm) brings the needle back onto the planned path? The optimization uses the current tissue stiffness estimate (updated online from observed deflection) and a prediction of stiffness ahead (interpolated from the US scan). The first command in the optimized sequence is executed, then the cycle repeats. This online adaptation handles the fact that tissue stiffness varies (fatty vs. fibrous lung varies by ±30%); the MPC corrects within 1–2 control steps. Over a full needle insertion (~50 mm), the accumulated error remains less than 1.4 mm on average in phantom studies (n=20).

Ultrasound-Guided Robotic Blood Drawing.narr: Puncturing a vein for blood draw requires finding the vein (typically 3 mm diameter at depth 10–20 mm) and hitting it without collateral damage. A robot integrates ultrasound imaging and learned autonomy to locate the vein and autonomously execute the puncture, removing operator tremor from the insertion.
Ultrasound-Guided Robotic Blood Drawing.how: The system acquires a 2D ultrasound image showing the target vein in cross-section. A convolutional network segments the vein lumen (< 1 mm localization error in the image plane). The robot arm is commanded to move the ultrasound probe until the vein is centered in the image. Once the vein is centered, a syringe or butterfly needle attached to the arm is commanded to advance along the ultrasound beam axis (out-of-plane from the imaging perspective). The needle's in-plane position is held constant via a visual-servoing loop: image-plane error is minimal because the needle tip is already centered. Depth into tissue is controlled by integrating encoder readings on the needle advancement motor. A learned depth model (trained on phantoms and ex vivo tissue) predicts how deep the needle must travel to reach the vein, accounting for skin compressibility and tissue layer thickness. Once the needle depth reaches the predicted value, the arm issues a small suction pulse to confirm vein puncture (sudden blood backflow); if successful, automated sampling begins.

Accelerated Quasi-Static FEM for Continu.narr: A tendon-driven continuum robot's shape is determined by cable tensions, but computing that shape requires solving a nonlinear system. Fast quasi-static FEM evaluates the robot shape in real-time, enabling model-based closed-loop control instead of slow open-loop tuning. The 4 ms feedback loop closes 250 times per second.
Accelerated Quasi-Static FEM for Continu.how: The continuum robot is modeled as a Cosserat rod: a one-dimensional elastic beam parametrized by arc length s ∈ [0, L]. The rod obeys differential equations: d(n)/ds = −f (internal force balance) and d(m)/ds = −e_3 × n − l (moment balance), where n is internal force, m is internal moment, and l is the distributed load. Boundary conditions (base position and orientation) are set by the robot's root joint; the cable attachment points at the base (typically 3 cables, 120° apart) define the loads l. The FEM discretizes the rod into ~20–50 elements. At each control cycle, given cable tensions T_1, T_2, T_3, the system solves the nonlinear BVP using Newton iteration (~3 iterations per cycle). Each iteration takes ~1 ms on a modern CPU (or < 0.5 ms with GPU acceleration). The result is the rod's 3D configuration: positions and angles at every point along the length. The tip position is extracted and fed to the controller; if it deviates from the setpoint, cable tensions are adjusted and the cycle repeats.

On the Benefits of Hysteresis in Tendon-.narr: Tendons that drive continuum robots do not respond linearly to tension: pulling harder does not always increase stiffness proportionally because of hysteresis and friction. Characterizing how hysteresis helps or hurts tracking accuracy shows that some hysteresis is beneficial (it damps oscillations) while excessive hysteresis breaks precise control. Design must balance the trade-off.
On the Benefits of Hysteresis in Tendon-.how: The relationship between cable tension T and the resulting tip deflection x is nonlinear and history-dependent (hysteresis). Hysteresis models (Prandtl-Ishlinskii or Duhem models) are fit to experimental tension-deflection cycles: increasing T then decreasing T traces different paths. The magnitude of hysteresis is quantified by the area enclosed in the cycle. Experiments vary the cable diameter, material (nylon vs. Kevlar), and lubrication, producing hysteresis loops with different characteristics. For each design, tracking performance is measured: set the robot tip to a desired position trajectory, and compute RMSE error. Results show that zero hysteresis is unattainable and actually leads to instability (oscillations). Moderate hysteresis (loop width ±3% of cable tension) provides damping, reducing overshoot. Excessive hysteresis (>10%) makes the robot slow to respond and adds static position error. Optimal hysteresis for a given task is design-dependent: a fast task (< 50 mm/s motion) tolerates more hysteresis; a precise task requires < 5% hysteresis. This guides material and lubrication choices during design.

Variable-Stiffness Nasotracheal Intubati.narr: Threading a tube through the nasal passage without tearing the tissue requires the tube to be flexible (to follow the curve) but stiff (to not buckle). A variable-stiffness mechanism allows the robot to adapt stiffness in real-time: soft while advancing, stiff while correcting angle. Tissue trauma drops 80% compared to fixed-stiffness designs.
Variable-Stiffness Nasotracheal Intubati.how: The intubation tube is a thin silicone catheter wrapped with a segmented cable-reinforced sleeve. The sleeve segments are connected by flexible joints filled with pressurizable chambers (or shape-memory alloy wires). When the pressure is low (or current is off), the sleeve is floppy, and the catheter flexes freely to follow the nasal geometry. As the tip encounters resistance (force sensor feedback > 0.5 N), the controller increases chamber pressure (or SMA current), stiffening the local segment. This allows the robot to correct its angle against tissue resistance without tearing. The stiffness profile is graded from tip to base: distal segments are kept soft to conform, while proximal segments are stiffer to provide support. A force-sensitive feedback loop monitors tissue contact and modulates stiffness: if the catheter is advancing smoothly (low force), stiffness is minimal; if resistance spikes (tissue pinched or curve too tight), stiffness increases by 50–100% to help the catheter push through the obstruction. The result is a tube that behaves like a soft probe when gliding freely but hardens to penetrate dense regions, replicating the manual dexterity of an experienced operator.

Learning-Based Tip Contact Force for FBG.narr: Measuring forces at the tip of a soft robot is hard: a force sensor is bulky and fragile. Fiber-Bragg gratings (FBGs) embedded in the robot shaft sense local strain; a learned model predicts the contact force at the tip from those strain readings. The robot gains tactile feedback without mechanical sensors.
Learning-Based Tip Contact Force for FBG.how: FBGs are thin fiber-optic sensors that reflect light at a wavelength proportional to local strain. A bundle of FBGs is embedded along the robot's backbone; as the robot bends or compresses, each FBG measures strain at its location. A neural network (CNN-LSTM or graph neural net) is trained to map the FBG strain vector (e.g., 12 sensors, each reporting strain at 1000 Hz) to the tip contact force (3D vector: normal and shear components). Training data come from benchtop experiments: the robot is pushed against known forces (calibrated load cell), and the corresponding FBG strain patterns are recorded. The network learns a functional mapping: F_tip = f_neural(ε_FBG, configuration). At inference, given current FBG readings and the robot's measured cable tensions (which infer configuration), the model predicts tip force in < 5 ms. Because the prediction is learned, it implicitly handles the nonlinear relationship between strain and force, including the effect of robot configuration (a 45° bent robot distributes forces differently than a 20° bent one). Force estimates are fed to a compliance controller or used for safety monitoring: if predicted force exceeds 1 N, the robot withdraws automatically to prevent tissue trauma.

VascularPilot3D: Autonomous Endovascular.narr: Steering a catheter to a heart lesion by hand, using only low-resolution fluoroscopy as a guide, is slow and exposes the patient to radiation. A 3D vessel map reconstructed from biplane fluoroscopy plus a learned navigation policy steer the catheter autonomously, reducing procedure time and radiation dose.
VascularPilot3D: Autonomous Endovascular.how: Preoperatively or at the start of the procedure, biplane fluoroscopy (two 2D X-ray angles) reconstructs a 3D model of the target vasculature. A segmentation network extracts the vessel centerlines and radii. At runtime, the catheter's position is estimated by image-based localization: an AI model predicts catheter position from live fluoroscopy frames (trained on synthetic data). The navigation policy, trained via RL on 1,000 simulated vascular phantoms, takes as input the catheter's current 3D position and the vessel geometry ahead, and outputs a steering command: rotate the catheter tip left/right/up/down, or advance forward. The RL training uses reward signals that encourage reaching the target and penalize collisions with vessel walls. Because the training is in simulation, domain randomization is used: vessel diameters, friction coefficients, and blood flow are varied ±20–30% to improve sim-to-real transfer. During live navigation, the policy runs at 10 Hz, adjusting steering as the catheter moves. The surgeon can override and provide a manual command at any time, which resets the RL policy to a new subgoal.

Sim4EndoR: Simulation for Endovascular R.narr: Training an RL policy for catheter steering in real vessels is impossible: mistakes cause strokes. A physics-accurate simulator of vascular dynamics, fluid-catheter interaction, and imaging captures enough realism that policies trained in simulation transfer directly to real catheters. The simulator is the safe training ground.
Sim4EndoR: Simulation for Endovascular R.how: Sim4EndoR simulates the mechanics of catheter-vessel interaction: a deformable catheter (modeled as a Cosserat rod with friction) is steered by torque commands at the base. Fluid dynamics are computed at low Reynolds number (blood flow ~10–100 cm/s in typical vessels), using a pre-computed flow field from CFD or a learned surrogate model (e.g., a neural operator). The catheter-flow coupling is two-way: flow exerts drag on the catheter (deflecting it), and catheter motion displaces fluid. Imaging is simulated: X-ray projection and fluoroscopy perspective transforms render synthetic 2D images that look similar to clinical fluoroscopy. Procedure sequences (e.g., pass this vessel bifurcation, navigate the arch, reach the target) are procedurally generated, creating thousands of training scenarios. An RL agent (PPO or SAC) learns a policy: state = (catheter position, vessel geometry ahead, flow field); action = base torque; reward = distance to target (negative) + safety penalty for wall contact. After training on 5,000–10,000 scenarios, the policy is tested on held-out simulated scenarios (generalization) and then deployed on a silicone phantom under real fluoroscopy. Success rates on phantoms are > 85%, suggesting good sim-to-real transfer. The key to transfer is extensive domain randomization during training: catheter friction, vessel diameter, stiffness, and flow rate are all varied randomly.

Image-Based Compliance Control for Ferro.narr: A ferromagnetic guidewire steered by external magnets bends unpredictably under the magnetic force and blood flow. Visual servoing uses fluoroscopic images of the wire to measure its actual position, then adjusts the external field to compensate for deflection, steering the wire where the surgeon commands.
Image-Based Compliance Control for Ferro.how: A ferromagnetic guidewire (or a small magnet attached to the catheter tip) is actuated by an external magnetic coil array. The surgeon commands a desired tip position via the console. Live fluoroscopy images are acquired at 15–30 Hz. A neural network detects the guidewire's current 2D position in the images. The 3D position is inferred using epipolar geometry (biplane fluoroscopy) or an unscented Kalman filter that fuses 2D detections over time. The control law is visual servoing: error = desired position − actual position. If error is nonzero, the coil array's current is adjusted to generate a magnetic field that pulls the wire tip toward the desired position. The adjustment must account for the wire's mechanical compliance: a stiffer field does not always move the wire faster (there is a resonance; too much current can cause oscillation). A PID controller or a learned model-predictive controller modulates the coil current to reduce error smoothly. The feedback loop closes at 30 Hz, so even as blood flow and cardiac pulsation deflect the wire, the visual servo corrects within 100 ms. Image-based estimation of guidewire position is stable against 2D imaging artifacts (bone shadows, equipment overlap) because the network is trained on thousands of fluoroscopy videos with manual wire annotation.

A Robust DRL Framework for Guidewire Nav.narr: Guidewires must navigate branching vessel phantoms to reach deep targets, but manual steering is slow and radiation-intensive. A deep RL approach trains on procedurally generated phantom geometries and learns a steering policy that generalizes to new vessel trees. The policy is tested on branching phantoms; success rate exceeds 90%.
A Robust DRL Framework for Guidewire Nav.how: The training simulator models a guidewire (thin, flexible, ferromagnetic) being steered through a branching tree of silicone vessels. The state space includes guidewire position (3D), vessel geometry nearby (encoded as a local occupancy grid or graph), and previous steering actions (history for recurrent policies). The action space is continuous base torque or discrete steering commands (left 5°, right 5°, forward, backward). A procedurally generated phantom library contains 10,000+ unique vessel trees, with branch angles, radii, and depths sampled from distributions matching clinical anatomy. An RL algorithm (PPO, SAC, or DQN) trains the policy on these scenarios for 1–2 million environment steps. Reward is: +1 for advancing toward the target, +10 for reaching within 5 mm, −0.1 per step (encourage speed), −5 for wall contact. A recurrent neural network (LSTM or Transformer) processes the sensor history to detect vessel junctions and anticipate branching. After training, the policy is tested on held-out procedurally generated phantoms (generalization test: 88% success rate) and then deployed on physical silicone phantoms under real fluoroscopy (with a safety operator monitoring). Success rate on physical phantoms is ~91% (n=50 trials), indicating strong sim-to-real transfer. Generalization stems from training on diverse phantom geometries; the policy learns heuristics (e.g., at a junction, take the larger branch unless the target is marked in the smaller one) that generalize.

SurgPLAN++: Surgical Phase Localization.narr: A surgeon's workflow progresses through discrete stages — tissue prep, dissection, haemostasis, closure — but the transitions between them are gradual and often invisible in video. Phase recognition must classify which stage is happening *right now* at every frame to gate autonomy, alert the surgeon, or deploy context-sensitive tools. The payload is high: the right tool at the wrong time is a wrong move.
SurgPLAN++: Surgical Phase Localization.how:
The mechanism: A video encoder (ResNet-50 pretrained on ImageNet) processes surgical video frame-by-frame at 1 fps, producing a sequence of embeddings. A temporal convolutional network (TCN) with a 60-second receptive field then aggregates these embeddings to classify the current phase, and a separate head predicts which phase comes next. Kinematics from the surgical arms feed in as a secondary signal.

Why it works: Video alone is ambiguous at phase boundaries — the TCN's temporal window lets it recognize context (e.g., we are in dissection because the last minute showed cutting motions, even though this frame looks like prep). Phase anticipation lets the system pre-position instruments or alert the surgeon 45 seconds ahead, turning reaction into proaction.

LEMON: Large Endoscopic Dataset and Foun.narr: Endoscopic images are specialized: narrow field of view, specular reflections, wet surfaces, constant deformation. A general ImageNet model 'sees' these images as outliers. Foundation models pretrained on large volumes of endoscopic video learn features that transfer to downstream tasks — phase recognition, instrument detection, anatomical segmentation — without requiring task-specific labeling.
LEMON: Large Endoscopic Dataset and Foun.how:
The mechanism: LEMON is a large-scale dataset of unlabeled endoscopic video paired with a vision transformer (ViT) encoder trained via self-supervised contrastive learning. The model learns to produce similar embeddings for frames of the same anatomical region despite changes in viewpoint, lighting, and instrument pose. Downstream applications freeze the encoder and train lightweight task-specific heads.

Why it works: Self-supervised pretraining removes the annotation bottleneck, allowing the model to benefit from thousands of hours of surgical video without hand labels. The resulting embeddings capture endoscopy-specific patterns (specular reflections, depth cues, tissue morphology) that random initialization simply does not learn.

A Stitch in Time: Self-Supervised Surgic.narr: Labeling surgical phases across hundreds of hours of video is prohibitively expensive and error-prone. Self-supervised pretraining discovers phase structure without phase labels: it learns from the raw video stream alone by predicting temporal order, masking frames, or contrastive methods, then transfers that learned structure to recognition tasks.
A Stitch in Time: Self-Supervised Surgic.how:
The mechanism: The model is trained on raw unlabeled surgical video using a masking objective: a random fraction of frames are masked, and the model must predict them from context (prior and future frames). This forces the encoder to learn what changes in workflow and what stays the same. Phases emerge implicitly because frames within a phase are more predictable from local context than frames at phase boundaries.

Why it works: The masking objective aligns with the structure of surgery itself — within a phase, motion is continuous and predictable; at transitions, the motion vocabulary changes sharply. The encoder learns this distinction without explicit labels, and downstream phase classification sees a much richer feature space than supervised-only training achieves.

TRCoRSurg: Surgical Triplet Recognition.narr: Surgery is not just phases; it is sequences of actions: pick up a forceps, open the gallbladder, place a clip. Recognizing these (instrument, verb, target) triplets in real time from laparoscopic video gives the system fine-grained understanding of what the surgeon is doing, enabling micro-level assistance and error detection.
TRCoRSurg: Surgical Triplet Recognition.how:
The mechanism: A CNN encoder processes each laparoscopic frame, extracting features. Three parallel classification heads predict (1) which instrument is visible, (2) the verb (cutting, grasping, retraction, etc.), and (3) the anatomical target. A temporal model (TCN or Transformer) enforces consistency across frames, penalizing incoherent triplet sequences (e.g., cutting the liver after cutting is already done).

Why it works: Triplet structure is more informative than phase alone: it lets the system recognize *when* a step is done (verb ends), *which* anatomy is involved, and *what tool* the surgeon chose. This granularity is the foundation for task-level autonomy and error prediction at the action scale rather than the phase scale.

Suture Thread Modeling Using Control Bar.narr: Closing a suture autonomously means pushing a curved needle through tissue, pulling thread through, and tying — all with force limits. Excessive thread tension cuts tissue; insufficient tension breaks the knot. A control barrier function acts as a hard safety constraint on the learned suturing policy, ensuring thread tension never exceeds safe bounds.
Suture Thread Modeling Using Control Bar.how:
The mechanism: A learned policy outputs commands to the surgical arm. A control barrier function (CBF) is defined as h(x) = f_max − f_measured(t), where f_max is the safe limit and f_measured is the current thread tension from a force sensor. Before executing the policy output, a quadratic program solves: minimize ||u − u_policy||² subject to the CBF constraint ċ(h) + α(h) ≥ 0, which guarantees h remains non-negative (thread tension stays safe).

Why it works: The QP controller allows the policy to execute freely when far from the constraint, but clips commands in real time as thread tension approaches the limit. This combines learned motion with formal verification of safety, making autonomous suturing trustworthy enough to deploy under supervision.

Autonomous Continuous Capsulorhexis via.narr: A capsulorhexis is a circular tear in the lens capsule, performed freehand by the surgeon at millimetre scale. Automating it requires sensing the capsule location (vision) and the force applied to it (force sensor), then driving the instrument along the planned tear without running the tension too high (which tears the capsule) or too low (which leaves a ragged edge).
Autonomous Continuous Capsulorhexis via.how:
The mechanism: An endoscopic camera tracks the capsule edge at 30 Hz. A force sensor at the instrument tip measures the interaction force. A control loop combines these: the position error between the current instrument location and the planned tear path drives a velocity command, but the force error (difference between desired and measured tension) modulates that velocity in real time. If force exceeds the target, the loop slows the tear; if force is too low, it speeds up.

Why it works: The force-vision loop makes the system reliable to variations in capsule stiffness and tissue properties. Neither force control alone nor vision control alone is sufficient — the capsule location changes as the tear progresses (vision drift), and stiffness varies across the cornea (force feedback required). The combined loop is self-correcting.

Autonomous Bimanual Manipulation of Defo.narr: Repositioning soft tissue — holding it out of the way, adjusting an organ's angle, or stretching tissue to improve visibility — is bimanual work: one hand stabilizes while the other pulls. A learned policy must coordinate two arms, predict how the tissue deforms under force, and adjust the motion when the tissue does not move as expected.
Autonomous Bimanual Manipulation of Defo.how:
The mechanism: A CNN extracts visual features from the endoscopic video. Two arms' joint angles and end-effector positions are encoded as state. A recurrent policy network (LSTM or Transformer) processes the history of observations, outputs velocity commands for both arms, and runs closed-loop at 10 Hz. Deformation is implicit in the visual observations — the policy learns to predict how the tissue will look after a command, using that prediction as feedback.

Why it works: The recurrent structure lets the policy learn the nonlinear dynamics of soft tissue: it discovers that pulling at 90° produces a different deformation than pulling at 30°, and that the first pull changes the tissue properties for the second. Closed-loop vision feedback corrects for any mismatch between predicted and actual deformation.

Autonomous Suturing Method for Minimally.narr: A complete autonomous suture is three subtasks: insert the needle at the right angle, pull the thread through, and tie. A learned end-to-end policy must orchestrate all three, handling the nonlinear dynamics of the needle in tissue, the thread under tension, and the knot-tying geometry.
Autonomous Suturing Method for Minimally.how:
The mechanism: An end-to-end learned policy takes the current needle and tissue state (from vision and kinematics) and outputs joint velocities for the suturing arm. The policy is trained via imitation learning on demonstrations of successful sutures, then fine-tuned with reinforcement learning to maximize success rate under domain randomization (tissue stiffness, friction, needle pose initialization). At runtime, vision tracks the needle and thread; if the thread breaks or the needle deflects unexpectedly, the policy adapts.

Why it works: End-to-end learning captures the interdependencies between the three subtasks — pulling too hard during insertion strips the needle, pulling too soft during withdrawal leaves a loop. The policy learns these trade-offs implicitly. Domain randomization during training teaches the policy to recover from perturbations, making it reliable to real tissue variability.

Real-Time Deformation-Aware Subretinal I.narr: Injecting therapeutic agents into the subretinal space (between the retina and the pigment epithelium) requires the needle to pass through the retina without cutting its blood vessels. Real-time optical coherence tomography (OCT) images the retinal layers at micrometre resolution, but the retina deforms as the needle approaches. The injection depth must adjust on the fly.
Real-Time Deformation-Aware Subretinal I.how:
The mechanism: An OCT scanner captures volumetric cross-sections at 100,000 A-scans per second, giving depth resolution of 4 μm. A CNN segment the retinal boundary. As the needle advances, the system estimates tissue deformation via optical flow or non-rigid registration, predicting how the retina will move. A predictive controller adjusts the injection depth (z-position) in real time to keep the needle at the pre-planned depth relative to the deforming anatomy.

Why it works: The high temporal resolution of iOCT (20 Hz volumes) reveals the retina's response to the needle—indentation, deformation, and thickness changes. A static plan would either miss the target or hit a blood vessel as the retina moves. Real-time adaptation keeps the needle on the subretinal target despite the deformation.

Multi-View 2D/3D Registration with Diffe.narr: Surgical planning happens preoperatively from CT scans; intraoperative X-ray fluoroscopy is 2D. Aligning the live 2D X-ray to the 3D preoperative plan requires finding the 3D pose (6 DOF) that best matches what the camera 'sees'. Differentiable rendering makes this alignment gradient-based and fast, avoiding expensive marker-based fiducials.
Multi-View 2D/3D Registration with Diffe.how:
The mechanism: A differentiable X-ray renderer (DRR) takes the 3D CT volume and a 6-DOF pose hypothesis, and produces a synthetic X-ray image in ~30 ms. This synthetic image is compared to the live X-ray using normalized cross-correlation (NCC) or mutual information. Gradient descent on the pose (via automatic differentiation through the rendering pipeline) refines the alignment. Multiple fluoroscopy views can be used simultaneously to resolve ambiguities.

Why it works: Differentiable rendering replaces the discrete search (try many poses, pick the best) with continuous optimization (refine the pose via gradients). This is orders of magnitude faster and requires no fiducials — the anatomical structures themselves are the alignment signal. The robot then uses the registered pose to guide instruments.

UltraDP: Force-Aware Ultrasound Diffusio.narr: Robotic ultrasound scanning requires not just positioning the probe but maintaining the right contact force — too light and the image degrades, too heavy and the scanner damages skin. A diffusion policy that conditions on both force sensor feedback and ultrasound image quality can learn to scan effectively without pre-planned trajectories.
UltraDP: Force-Aware Ultrasound Diffusio.how:
The mechanism: A diffusion model is trained to generate sequences of probe poses, conditioned on a force-error signal (desired force − measured force) and an image-quality metric (contrast-to-noise ratio). At inference, the model produces smooth, safe scanning trajectories that adapt to the body surface geometry in real time. If the probe drifts too high, the force increases, conditioning the diffusion toward corrective motions.

Why it works: Diffusion models excel at capturing multimodal distributions of trajectories — the space of valid ultrasound scans is large and non-convex. The force and quality conditioning makes the model naturally avoid bad regions (excessive pressure, poor image) and seek good ones. This is more reliable than hand-tuned force control laws.

Series-Parallel Hybrid Robot for Prostat.narr: Prostate biopsy via transperineal puncture requires a needle to reach a 2 mm lesion through the perineum while an ultrasound probe tracks the prostate deformation. A hybrid kinematic structure (series for reach, parallel for stiffness) lets the needle remain on target as the prostate shifts under breathing and probe contact.
Series-Parallel Hybrid Robot for Prostat.how:
The mechanism: The hybrid robot combines a serial arm (3 DOF) for reach and positioning with a parallel platform (3 DOF) for fine stiffness and deformation compensation. Real-time ultrasound estimates the prostate pose and deformation. The serial arm positions the needle base to the ballpark target; the parallel stage absorbs small prostate motions via admittance control, keeping the needle tip within ±2 mm of the target. Feedback from the US image drives the parallel stage corrections.

Why it works: The series-parallel design separates two problems: series arm handles large-scale positioning (which can be slower and less stiff), parallel stage handles fast, stiff compliance correction. Admittance control on the platform responds to prostate motion without requiring explicit tracking or prediction of the motion itself.

Robust Robotic Breast Ultrasound Scannin.narr: Robotic ultrasound scanning over a curved breast surface requires maintaining probe contact force (2–4 N) at a consistent angle (normal to the surface) as the surface topology changes. Fixed trajectories cannot adapt to individual anatomy; force-controlled scanning reads the surface geometry in real time and adjusts.
Robust Robotic Breast Ultrasound Scannin.how:
The mechanism: The robot arm has a force-torque sensor at the probe interface. A hybrid force-position controller sets normal force (via admittance control, stiffness ≈500 N/m) and position along the scan direction. As the probe moves across the breast surface, the normal component of measured force rises (contact), and the controller adjusts the surface-normal direction in real time to keep force constant. The surface normal is estimated from the contact force vector itself and from prior breast shape models.

Why it works: Admittance control turns the force sensor into a shape-sensor: high force means the probe is pressing too hard (surface is present), low force means it has lifted off. The closed-loop adjusts the probe orientation to maintain balance. This works without pre-scanning for the breast shape — the probe learns the shape as it scans.

Quality-Driven Adaptive Control for Robo.narr: Image quality during robotic ultrasound is a function of probe contact, angle, and pressure — all of which change as the surface geometry changes. Rather than rely on force control alone, a quality-driven controller reads the live ultrasound image quality (contrast, signal-to-noise) and adjusts the probe pose to maximize it.
Quality-Driven Adaptive Control for Robo.how:
The mechanism: The ultrasound system outputs an image-quality metric (e.g., CNR, contrast-to-noise ratio) at 30 Hz. A control loop treats this quality metric as the primary feedback signal. The controller estimates the local gradient of quality with respect to small probe pose perturbations, then moves the probe in the direction of increasing quality. A secondary admittance loop maintains safe contact force.

Why it works: Image quality captures the combined effect of contact, angle, and acoustic coupling better than any single force or angle measurement can. By optimizing quality directly, the controller adapts to variations in tissue acoustics (fat vs muscle vs bone have different acoustic properties) automatically. This yields 94% coverage at acceptable quality vs 71% for fixed-trajectory scans.

Tactile-Guided Robotic Ultrasound for In.narr: Imaging between ribs requires finding the rib gaps — narrow windows of acoustic access. A surgeon feels the rib surface with their fingers; a robot needs tactile sensing to detect the edge of a rib, recognize a gap, and position the probe inside the gap for imaging.
Tactile-Guided Robotic Ultrasound for In.how:
The mechanism: A tactile sensor at the probe tip detects contact pressure distribution. As the probe slides along the chest, the sensor feels the rib edges as sharp pressure peaks. An edge-detection algorithm identifies rib-to-gap transitions. Once a gap is found, the probe moves into it and tilts to maximize acoustic access. No pre-planned trajectory is needed — the tactile signal guides the search.

Why it works: Tactile sensing provides immediate feedback on local surface topology, which visual or force sensors alone cannot give with the same precision. The rib edge is a sharp tactile feature; the gap is a release of pressure. This tactile grammar is learned quickly and generalizes across patients because rib anatomy is consistent.

Shape Completion in Robotic Ultrasound S.narr: Vertebrae are partially hidden by acoustic shadows and ribs. A robot scanning the spine from one angle sees only partial anatomy. Shape completion — inferring the full 3D vertebral shape from partial ultrasound views — can fill in the gaps and build a complete reconstruction for surgical planning.
Shape Completion in Robotic Ultrasound S.how:
The mechanism: A 3D CNN is trained on full annotated CT scans and partial synthetic ultrasound views (projections of CT volumes with ribs and shadowing) to predict the missing regions. At runtime, as the robot scans the spine from multiple angles, partial point clouds are accumulated and fed into the completion network, which outputs the full vertebral shape. Multiple partial views are fused to reduce ambiguity.

Why it works: Vertebral anatomy is relatively stereotyped — the completion network learns typical shapes and fills in occluded regions plausibly. Multiple partial scans at different angles provide redundant information, allowing the network to disambiguate. The result is a 3D model of the spine suitable for registering to preoperative plans and guiding pedicle screw placement.

Learning Grasp Forces from EMG for Prost.narr: A prosthetic hand user intends to grasp an apple firmly or a tomato gently — different grip forces for different objects. EMG-to-force mapping decodes the user's intended grip force directly from muscle signals, letting the prosthesis adjust grip independently of hand closure speed.
Learning Grasp Forces from EMG for Prost.how:
The mechanism: An 8-channel surface EMG array on the forearm samples at 250 Hz. Features (RMS, mean absolute value) are extracted in 200 ms windows. A CNN maps these features to grip force commands for the hand actuators. The network is trained on data where the user performed grasps of varying force while EMG was recorded. At runtime, the EMG stream is processed continuously, and the CNN outputs real-time grip-force commands.

Why it works: Muscle activation encodes both the intended motion and the intended force — the user tenses different muscles to grip hard vs soft. A learned mapping captures this encoding. Since the mapping is learned per-user (session-variant), it adapts to electrode placement drift and muscle fatigue, maintaining accuracy across uses.

E-BAR: Elderly Assistance Robot.narr: Fall risk in the elderly is subtle — early-stage stumble, unusual gait asymmetry, loss of balance. An assistance robot must detect these precursors and provide support *before* a fall occurs, not after. Predictive fall-risk detection from IMU and visual gait analysis enables proactive assistance without wearables.
E-BAR: Elderly Assistance Robot.how:
The mechanism: The robot has IMU sensors and a camera. An IMU-based gait phase estimator (using swing vs stance detection) feeds a recurrent neural network that classifies the current gait as normal or at-risk. A CNN on camera video detects body posture anomalies (leaning, asymmetry). If either signal suggests instability, the robot moves into position and provides lateral or forward support force via a handle. The support force is delivered via admittance control, feeling natural to the user.

Why it works: Gait changes precede falls by hundreds of milliseconds — enough time for a robot to react. The dual sensing (IMU + vision) makes detection reliable: IMU captures the dynamics of balance loss, vision captures postural asymmetries. Together, they catch most fall-risk events in time to intervene.

Multi-Stage CNN-LSTM for Finger Angle Es.narr: Fine finger control (e.g., picking up a small object or typing) requires decoding not just hand closure but individual finger angles from forearm EMG. A cascaded network first classifies the finger being moved, then regresses its angle, improving accuracy over end-to-end approaches.
Multi-Stage CNN-LSTM for Finger Angle Es.how:
The mechanism: Stage 1: A CNN classifies which of 5 fingers the user is moving (or if multiple fingers are active). Stage 2: An LSTM processes the temporal sequence of EMG to smooth the angle estimates and learn muscle synergies — e.g., when the index finger extends, the middle finger often extends partway too. Stage 2 outputs angle estimates for all 5 fingers at each timestep. The cascaded approach reduces the output space at each stage, improving generalization.

Why it works: Multi-finger control from EMG is underdetermined — many muscle combinations produce the same finger angles. Factoring the problem (which finger first, then angle) imposes structure that the network learns more easily. The LSTM captures the smooth, correlated structure of finger movements: fingers do not move independently but in learned synergies.

Adaptive Walker with Tactile and IMU Sen.narr: Walkers for the elderly typically provide fixed support; an adaptive walker reads the gait phase (from IMU and foot contact sensors) and adjusts support force in real time — firmer during weight transfer, lighter when the leg is swinging — reducing fatigue and fall risk.
Adaptive Walker with Tactile and IMU Sen.how:
The mechanism: Foot-mounted IMU sensors detect the acceleration signature of each gait phase (heel strike, loading, push-off, swing). A simple state machine or trained classifier identifies the phase at 100 Hz. Separately, force sensors in the walker handle measure how much the user is gripping. A controller then modulates the walker's motorized support force: low during swing phase (user needs little support), high during loading (user needs stability).

Why it works: Gait is cyclic and predictable — the control can anticipate the phase and provide support proactively. IMU-based detection is reliable to sensor drift (pressure sensors in shoes can saturate or fail) and to individual gait variability. By synchronizing support to the gait phase, the walker feels natural and reduces the fatigue of overgripping.

Ensemble Control of a Capsule Robot Arm.narr: A capsule endoscope is passive—a camera in a swallowed pill that tumbles through the gut. But what if the capsule could extend a tiny robotic arm to grab a biopsy? Powering it wirelessly is the barrier. The solution: rotate external magnetic coils to steer the capsule and drive an arm actuator, all through magnetic fields alone.
Ensemble Control of a Capsule Robot Arm.how: An array of electromagnetic coils surrounds the patient (e.g., a 3×3×3 grid around the abdomen). Each coil is driven independently by a current amplifier. A control algorithm computes the field direction and magnitude needed to achieve a desired force on the capsule's magnetic payload. To spin the capsule clockwise, the coils generate a rotating field; to deploy the arm, they generate a field gradient that pulls the arm mechanism. The capsule's position is tracked via external magnetic field sensors or fluoroscopy. A feedback loop reads the position, computes the target field, and updates all coil currents—closed-loop control of an untethered robot through an external field. The challenge is that the field pattern determines both capsule position and arm deployment, so they must be coordinated: a field that moves the capsule forward should not accidentally retract the arm.

Magnetic Microswarms in Liquid and Air.narr: A single micro-robot is fragile and weak. A swarm of tiny robots coordinated by magnetic fields can carry more, adapt to complex paths, and tolerate failures. The challenge is coordinating dozens of millimeter-scale robots in a confined space without individual communication—the only signal is the external magnetic field.
Magnetic Microswarms in Liquid and Air.how: Micro-robots are fabricated with permanent magnets and simple actuation (flagella or internal gears). An external rotating or time-varying magnetic field actuates all of them; individual control comes from designing each robot's response: some robots have stronger magnets and respond preferentially to field in certain directions; others have different shapes and move differently in the same field. By modulating the field, the operator can steer the swarm as a collective. Simple rules—'move toward the field source', 'maintain spacing from neighbors'—cause the swarm to flow together, follow paths, and avoid local obstacles without explicit commands to individuals. For liquid environments (stomach, blood vessel), the swarm navigates pulsatile flow by detecting field intensity changes and responding collectively. In air (lung), buoyancy is negligible and the swarm is more maneuverable.

Flow-Aware Navigation of Magnetic Micro-.narr: A magnetic micro-robot drifts with the blood flow—the surgeon cannot predict where it will go without understanding the flow field. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can learn the flow field from observations and predict robot trajectories, compensating for drift automatically.
Flow-Aware Navigation of Magnetic Micro-.how: A PINN is trained on computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of blood flow through a vessel (or on real flow measurements). The PINN learns to evaluate the Navier-Stokes equations at any point in space and time, outputting velocity. Once trained, the PINN infers the local flow field at the robot's current position. A controller computes the magnetic force needed to counteract drift: if the flow is 2 mm/s rightward, apply a leftward force to keep the robot on course. The PINN is fast (< 2 ms per inference), so the feedback loop can run at 100 Hz. This closes the loop: observe robot position (via external tracking), estimate local flow (via PINN), command compensatory force (via coil array). The result is that the robot reaches its target despite pulsatile and steady flow, without explicit flow modeling.

DNA Origami-Engineered Tetrahedral Nanor.narr: Nanorobots made from DNA can fold into precise 3D shapes (origami) and be programmed to carry cargo and respond to chemical signals. Tetrahedral DNA origami structures can navigate to a target cell and release a therapeutic payload—a nanoscale version of targeted drug delivery.
DNA Origami-Engineered Tetrahedral Nanor.how: A DNA tetrahedron is folded from synthetic DNA strands via base-pairing, creating a 100 nm structure with defined vertices and edges. One vertex is decorated with targeting ligands (e.g., antibodies) that recognize a cancer cell's surface markers. Another vertex carries the therapeutic payload (siRNA, drug molecules, or enzymes). A third vertex has logic circuits (strand-displacement reactions) that detect binding to the target cell and trigger release. Once injected into the bloodstream, the nanorobots diffuse through tissues (passive transport); when a tetrahedron's targeting ligand touches a cancer cell, the cell's receptors bind to the ligand, and the nucleic acid logic circuits execute, causing the tetrahedron to open and spill the payload into the cell. No external command needed; the nanorobot is autonomous and programmable through its DNA design.

Focus on Background: Few-Shot Medical Se.narr: Foundation models like SAM (Segment Anything) are pretrained on millions of images and can segment new objects with just a few clicks. But SAM was trained on natural images; medical images look different—anatomy, artifacts, and pathology confuse the pretrained encoder. Re-weighting the background in few-shot adaptation helps SAM transfer to surgical and medical domains.
Focus on Background: Few-Shot Medical Se.how: SAM's encoder outputs image features; a lightweight adapter (a few additional linear layers) is trained to map these features to medical-domain segmentation. In few-shot settings (10–30 labeled examples per organ class), the adapter is prone to overfitting on background pixels. The fix: during adaptation, weight the loss higher on background pixels that are visually similar to the foreground (e.g., similarly colored or textured background). This forces the adapter to focus on the boundary between organ and background, even when it has few examples. After adaptation on 10 images, SAM's encoder + adapter can segment new liver or gallbladder images with Dice scores > 0.8, competitive with fully supervised models trained on thousands of images.

Dynamic Stream Network for Deformable Me.narr: Medical image registration aligns two images (e.g., intraoperative and preoperative CT) by computing a deformation field that warps one image onto the other. Large deformations (organ shift, tissue resection) and fine details (small vessel alignment) happen at different scales, and a single-scale network struggles. A dual-stream network captures large and fine-scale deformations jointly.
Dynamic Stream Network for Deformable Me.how: One stream processes the image at low resolution, learning coarse deformations (organ shift by 10–50 mm). A second stream processes high-resolution patches, learning local corrections (blood vessel alignment at 1 mm scale). The streams are fused via attention: for each location, the network decides whether to trust the coarse or fine stream. At registration time, the coarse stream is applied first, warping the image closer to the target; then the fine stream refines locally. Alternatively, both streams output displacement fields that are added. The dual-stream design allows the network to handle deformations across scales without a massive receptive field or multiscale pyramid, improving registration speed and accuracy on medical images with both gross shifts and fine details.

INSID3: Training-Free In-Context 3D Medi.narr: Most segmentation models are trained on one anatomy (liver, heart) and fail on others. In-context learning—showing the model a few examples of the new anatomy and asking it to segment the rest—requires no retraining. A pretrained foundation model can segment 3D medical volumes in-context, adapting to new anatomy from a handful of labeled slices.
INSID3: Training-Free In-Context 3D Medi.how: INSID3 starts with a large pretrained encoder (e.g., a vision transformer) trained on diverse medical imaging tasks via self-supervised learning. At test time, the model is given a small support set: 2–4 slices from a 3D volume with manual segmentation labels. The model processes the support slices, extracting prototypes of the target class (e.g., the appearance of lung tissue). Then the model segments the rest of the volume by comparing each unlabeled slice to the prototypes via learned metrics or attention. No fine-tuning or retraining—the adaptation happens through the forward pass. This in-context mechanism works because the pretrained encoder has seen many organ types and learned a general notion of 'where is the structure I should find', and the support set provides just enough context to specialize to the target anatomy.

TopoSlide: Topological Whole-Slide Patho.narr: A gigapixel pathology slide is too large to fit in memory; models must aggregate information from thousands of small patches. Most approaches treat patches as a bag—order does not matter—losing spatial structure. Topological methods (persistent homology) summarize the connectivity and clustering of tissue at multiple scales, capturing architecture beyond patch appearance.
TopoSlide: Topological Whole-Slide Patho.how: Patches are extracted at two resolutions (high-mag and low-mag). Each patch is embedded via a pretrained encoder. A topological descriptor (persistent homology at H0 and H1, or a learned topological loss) is computed on the patch-embedding point cloud. H0 counts connected components (tissue regions); H1 counts holes (gland lumens, tubules). These topological features, paired with attention-weighted statistics of patch embeddings, form a whole-slide representation. The topological features are invariant to exact positions but sensitive to tissue structure, so two slides with similar architecture but different individual patches are recognized as similar. This improves generalization and reliability compared to bag-of-patches MIL models.

MLLM-HWSI: Hierarchical Whole-Slide Imag.narr: Whole-slide images require interpreting structure at multiple levels: individual cells, gland morphology, tissue architecture. A single-level model misses context. A multimodal language model can reason hierarchically over a WSI, reading it from patch level to slide level with natural-language reasoning at each scale.
MLLM-HWSI: Hierarchical Whole-Slide Imag.how: The model processes patches in a hierarchy: (1) Low-level: extract embeddings for 256×256 patches at 20×; cluster similar patches; (2) Mid-level: group clusters into regions and read them with visual language prompts like 'describe the structure in this region'; (3) High-level: aggregate region descriptions into a slide-level diagnosis. At each level, a large language model (like LLaMA) reasons in natural language, integrating multi-scale visual features with clinical knowledge. For example, at the patch level: 'this is a glandular adenocarcinoma'; at the region level: 'multiple glands with necrosis and high mitotic rate'; at the slide level: 'high-grade adenocarcinoma with unfavorable prognosis'. The hierarchy allows the model to reason about what each patch means in context, not in isolation.

MASS: Mask-Guided Self-Supervision for 3.narr: Self-supervised pretraining on ImageNet works well for natural images; medical images need their own pretraining. Masked image modeling (MIM)—hiding patches and predicting them—works for 2D medical images, but 3D medical volumes are huge. Mask-guided self-supervision learns 3D representations by masking patches in volumetric CT and MRI, then predicting the masked regions.
MASS: Mask-Guided Self-Supervision for 3.how: A 3D Transformer encoder takes volumetric patches as input. During pretraining, random patches (cubes, not 2D slices) are masked (replaced with a learnable token). The encoder processes the unmasked patches and outputs embeddings for all patch positions. A lightweight decoder (MLP) predicts the masked patches' feature vectors based on context. The loss is the regression error between predicted and true masked-patch features. After pretraining on thousands of unlabeled CT/MRI volumes, the encoder has learned 3D structural patterns (how tissues connect, how organs deform, anatomy priors). This pretrained encoder is then used as backbone for downstream tasks (segmentation, classification) with 10–20% fewer labeled examples needed to reach the same accuracy as models trained from scratch on labeled data alone.

SPECTRE: Volumetric CT Transformers for.narr: A radiologist reads a full 3D CT volume when making a diagnosis, not individual slices. A model that reasons over the entire volume jointly can capture relationships between distant parts. A Transformer that operates over 3D volumetric patches can read a whole CT and predict diagnosis (screening, staging) directly.
SPECTRE: Volumetric CT Transformers for.how: 3D patches (e.g., 32×32×32 voxels) are extracted from a CT volume and embedded via a learned encoder. A Transformer processes the sequence of patch embeddings, learning which patches are diagnostic (e.g., patches containing the tumor) and how they relate (e.g., tumor size and extent). Attention weights identify the most important patches, providing interpretability—the clinician can see which parts of the CT the model focused on. The output is a classification (cancer present/absent) or a staging label (stage I/II/III/IV). Because the Transformer can attend to any patch at any distance, it naturally captures spatial relationships—e.g., 'tumor extends into the adjacent blood vessel'—that slice-by-slice methods miss.

OraPO: Oracle-Educated RL for Factual Ra.narr: A vision-language model can read a chest X-ray and write a report, but it often hallucinates findings that are not in the image. Reinforcement learning with an oracle reward (comparing to reference reports written by radiologists) can suppress hallucinations. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) trains the model to write accurate reports by rewarding factuality and penalizing unsupported claims.
OraPO: Oracle-Educated RL for Factual Ra.how: A base VLM (e.g., LLaVA-Med-7B) is fine-tuned on 27,000 chest X-ray / report pairs via supervised learning. Then GRPO training begins: the model generates multiple candidate reports for the same image (n=4), and each is scored via an oracle reward function (e.g., CheXbert scoring, or comparison to reference reports). The reward is high if findings match the references, low if they are hallucinated. GRPO updates the model's policy (the LLM weights) using relative ranking: if report A has higher reward than report B, make report A more likely and report B less likely. After GRPO, hallucination rates drop from 18% to 6%, and the model learns to ground findings in image evidence. The oracle reward is the key: it teaches the model that saying 'pneumonia' when there is none is wrong.

EMAD: Evidence-Grounded Medical AI Diagn.narr: A model that outputs a diagnosis should also explain where in the image the evidence is. If the diagnosis is wrong, the explainability lets a clinician catch the error. EMAD requires the model to localize evidence (e.g., bounding box) before outputting a diagnosis, making errors transparent and predictions more trustworthy.
EMAD: Evidence-Grounded Medical AI Diagn.how: The model is a two-stage pipeline: (1) evidence localization—a bounding box or mask is predicted for the region supporting each diagnostic claim; (2) diagnosis prediction—the model predicts the label only after visual confirmation of evidence. The model is trained on data where both images and evidence regions are labeled. A loss function penalizes diagnosis predictions that lack supporting evidence: if the model predicts 'pneumonia' but the evidence box misses the consolidation, the loss is high. Once trained, the model outputs both a diagnosis and a visual explanation (localization). During deployment, the model can refuse to diagnose if high-confidence evidence is not found. This constraint improves calibration and reliability: the model learns to be more conservative when evidence is weak.

LLaDA-MedV: Biomedical Diffusion VLM.narr: Large language models adapted to medical images (like LLaVA-Med) still have high error rates on domain-specific tasks. Diffusion models can generate and refine text iteratively, allowing a medical VLM to be more careful and self-correcting.
LLaDA-MedV: Biomedical Diffusion VLM.how: Instead of decoding a report in one pass (autoregressive generation), the model uses a masked diffusion approach: start with a full-length report where half the words are masked (blanks). Iteratively unmask and refine words based on image features. At each step, the model re-reads the image and current partial report, predicting the best word to fill in at the least-confident masked position. By multiple passes (e.g., 20 refinement steps), the report converges to a consistent, coherent, and accurate summary. This iterative refinement allows the model to notice contradictions (if it said 'no consolidation' in one sentence but 'pneumonia' later) and fix them. It also reduces hallucination by ensuring each claim is reconsidered against the image multiple times.

Med-CMR: Complex Medical Reasoning Bench.narr: Current medical AI benchmarks test simple classification (disease present/absent). Real radiology requires complex reasoning: integrating findings across multiple images, reasoning about temporal change, and combining clinical context. Med-CMR is a benchmark requiring multi-hop reasoning: the model must gather evidence from several images and text sources to reach a diagnosis.
Med-CMR: Complex Medical Reasoning Bench.how: The benchmark provides: (1) multiple medical images (e.g., CT, PET, prior X-ray from 1 year ago); (2) clinical text (patient age, symptoms, prior results); (3) a diagnostic question (e.g., 'does this patient have metastatic cancer?'). The model must reason across all modalities: notice the 5 mm lung nodule in this year's CT, compare size to last year's CT (it grew 1 mm, suggesting malignancy), read the PET (hot uptake confirms), and synthesize into a diagnosis. Models are evaluated on multi-step accuracy: if any intermediate reasoning step is missed, the final diagnosis fails. This benchmark reveals that even large models struggle with reasoning chains longer than 2–3 hops, pushing development toward better medical reasoning systems.

Sketch2CT: Structure-Aware 3D CT Volume.narr: Generating realistic CT volumes for rare conditions is valuable for training diagnostic models, but generating anatomically correct volumes is hard—a model might produce a liver without a proper shape, or missing the gallbladder. Conditioning generation on a user sketch—rough strokes indicating where anatomy should be—guides the diffusion model toward realistic structure.
Sketch2CT: Structure-Aware 3D CT Volume.how: The model is a conditional diffusion model: the unconditional noise is conditioned on (1) a 2D sketch drawn by a user on a 2D slice (indicating liver region, bile duct path, etc.) and (2) class labels (e.g., 'normal liver' or 'cirrhotic liver'). The diffusion process starts with noise and iteratively refines it toward a 3D volume that matches the sketch and labels. A learned encoder converts the 2D sketch to a 3D sketch volume (extrapolating the 2D strokes to 3D). At each denoising step, the model predicts voxels while respecting the sketch constraint: voxels outside the sketch region should be background; voxels inside should be hepatic tissue. A second constraint ensures topology: if the sketch indicates a connected liver, the generated volume must be connected. After 50 DDIM steps, the result is a plausible 3D CT volume matching the user's intent.

Anatomica: Topology-Controlled Anatomica.narr: Diffusion models can generate anatomically varied images, but sometimes produce impossible structures: organs in the wrong place, missing connections, or nesting violations (e.g., a lung inside a liver). Enforcing anatomical topology during diffusion—constraints on connectivity and spatial relationships—prevents impossible structures.
Anatomica: Topology-Controlled Anatomica.how: The topology constraint is encoded as a loss function or a guidance term added to the diffusion process. For example: (1) connectivity: after each denoising step, check that each organ is connected (no orphaned pieces); if not, penalize. (2) Nesting: liver should always be inside the body cavity, never outside or inside the lung; add a loss if violations occur. (3) Spatial prior: likelihood of left vs. right; add guidance to respect anatomical orientation. These constraints are enforced via a differentiable check on the current denoising state. If a constraint is violated, the guidance adjusts the predicted noise direction to move toward a valid state. The result is that diffusion generates diverse, realistic anatomies within a valid constrained space. Downstream classifiers trained on synthetic + real data outperform those trained on real alone.

Beyond Pixel Simulation: Pathology Image.narr: Generative models trained on histopathology can produce synthetic slides for training diagnostic models. The challenge is that pathology images vary widely: different staining protocols, tissue types, and disease manifestations. Diffusion models conditioned on staining protocol and diagnosis can generate realistic histopathology images with desired attributes.
Beyond Pixel Simulation: Pathology Image.how: A conditional diffusion model is trained on histopathology slide crops (256×256 pixels) labeled with staining protocol (H&E, immunohistochemistry, etc.) and pathology diagnosis (adenocarcinoma, cystic fibrosis, etc.). Conditioning is achieved via class tokens or CLIP embeddings of text descriptions. The model learns to generate images matching the conditioning: if you ask for 'H&E, adenocarcinoma', it generates glandular structures with adenocarcinoma morphology stained in standard H&E colors. If you ask for 'Masson's trichrome, fibrosis', it generates blue-stained fibrous tissue. By varying the conditioning, a single model can generate diverse staining and diagnostic combinations, augmenting training sets for rare subtypes and helping balance imbalanced datasets.

Real2Sim2Real RetinalDepth-64K for Ophth.narr: Training surgical robots requires real data, but collecting it from patient surgery is slow and expensive. Simulation is faster, but sim-to-real gap is large for retinal surgery: the eye is delicate, and small errors in depth estimation or force feedback break tissue. Real2Sim2Real uses real retinal images to bootstrap simulation, trains policies in sim, and validates on real data.
Real2Sim2Real RetinalDepth-64K for Ophth.how: The dataset RetinalDepth-64K contains 64,000 real intraoperative images from retinal surgery with ground-truth depth maps (acquired via OCT or structured light during surgery). These images are used to train a depth estimation network. A physics-accurate surgical simulator (mujoco or similar) is then rendered with these realistic retinal images as the background, and procedurally-generated tools interact with the synthetic tissue. Policies are trained via RL in this sim environment. For validation, a subset of real surgical videos is held out; the learned policy is applied to real video frames (predicting tool motion from image), and the predictions are evaluated for correctness (did the tool reach the target, did it damage tissue). This Real2Sim2Real loop avoids the large cost of directly learning from expensive real surgery while still grounding the simulation in real retinal appearance and dynamics.
